AL.redemption: 3 years from sale (certificate holder); owner may redeem administratively for up to 3 years after that in some cases
AL.notes: County-run auctions (bid-down-interest or premium in some counties); some parcels sold via state land commissioner if unsold.

AK.redemption: None after foreclosure judgment; pre-foreclosure redemption while in tax-foreclosure status (varies by borough)
AK.notes: Alaska has no county government; foreclosure and sale is handled by boroughs and the state (unorganized borough).

AZ.returns: Up to 16% per annum, bid down at auction
AZ.notes: Online county auctions (bid-down-interest format) are common.

AR.redemption: None after the sale — the owner's right ends at 4:00 p.m. the last business day before it (A.C.A. § 26-37-202)
AR.statute: Arkansas Code Title 26, Ch. 37 (§§ 26-37-202 sale and conveyance, 26-37-203 contest window)
AR.notes: State-run through the Commissioner of State Lands, not individual counties. A separate 90-day window to contest the validity of the conveyance (§ 26-37-203) is a title risk rather than a redemption right — it earns the purchaser nothing and extends to two years after removal of disability for minors, the incapacitated, and wartime service members. COSL conveys by limited warranty deed and warrants nothing about title.

CA.redemption: Up until 5pm the last business day before the sale (5-year delinquency threshold)
CA.statute: California Revenue & Taxation Code, Div. 1, Pt. 6
CA.notes: County tax collector auctions (premium bid); excess proceeds claims process applies.

CO.returns: 9 points above federal discount rate, set annually; premium/bid-down format varies by county
CO.notes: Many counties run online lien auctions in Oct/Nov.

CT.returns: Statutory redemption penalty (~18%/yr equivalent) plus costs
CT.notes: Municipal (not county) tax collector sales — Connecticut has no county government.

DE.redemption: Limited statutory redemption in some municipalities; generally minimal post-sale
DE.statute: Delaware Code Title 9 (varies by county) / Title 25 for monition process
DE.notes: New Castle, Kent, and Sussex Counties each run sheriff or monition sales; process is judicial.

DC.returns: Up to 18% per annum plus fees
DC.notes: Single citywide annual tax sale run by the Office of Tax and Revenue.

FL.redemption: Lien: 2 years before deed application allowed. Deed: none once issued.
FL.notes: Two-stage system: county tax lien certificate sale, then a separate tax deed sale if the lien is unredeemed and the holder applies.

GA.returns: 20% premium first year, +10% each additional year
GA.statute: Official Code of Georgia Annotated Title 48, Ch. 4
GA.notes: County sheriff's sale (first Tuesday of the month); notice/barment process required to clear title.

HI.notes: Sales run at the county level (Honolulu, Hawaii, Maui, Kauai).

ID.redemption: None once county takes title (occurs 3 years after delinquency, before public auction)
ID.notes: County takes a tax deed administratively first, then auctions the property.

IL.returns: Up to 36% penalty per 6-month period (bid-down), 18% max per period at auction
IL.notes: Cook County and downstate counties run separate sale calendars; scavenger sale also exists for long-delinquent parcels.

IN.notes: County-run certificate sales; unsold liens may go to a commissioners' sale.

IA.notes: County treasurer auctions (bid-down of percentage of parcel acquired).

KS.redemption: None once judicial foreclosure completes (roughly 3+ years of delinquency)
KS.notes: Judicial in-rem foreclosure process run by the county; sheriff's sale for the deed.

KY.notes: County clerk sells certificates of delinquency; third-party purchasers can add fees.

LA.redemption: 3 years from sale (5 years for some blighted/adjudicated parcels)
LA.statute: Louisiana Revised Statutes Title 47, Subtitle III
LA.notes: Parish-level sales (Louisiana uses parishes instead of counties).

ME.redemption: 18 months from lien filing, before deed recorded
ME.returns: N/A — outright deed transfer after redemption period
ME.notes: Municipality (not county) holds the tax lien and can foreclose administratively.

MD.redemption: 6 months minimum before foreclosure action can start; up to 1 year+
MD.notes: County/city auctions; purchaser must file a foreclosure action to clear title.

MA.redemption: 6 months from sale/taking (often extends in practice via litigation)
MA.notes: Municipality sells the tax title or takes it directly; purchaser forecloses via Land Court.

MI.redemption: Forfeiture/foreclosure process ends redemption rights before auction (roughly 2 years of delinquency)
MI.notes: County (or state, via Dept. of Treasury in some cases) runs the foreclosure and auction.

MN.redemption: 3 years from judgment (5 years for homestead/ag land)
MN.notes: County auctions land after the state forfeiture process completes.

MS.notes: Chancery clerk runs the county sale; unredeemed liens convert to a deed to the purchaser.

MO.redemption: 1 year (2 years for some parcels) from sale
MO.returns: 10% per annum plus 8% on subsequent taxes paid
MO.notes: County collector auctions; purchaser must petition for a collector's deed after the redemption period.

MT.notes: County treasurer assigns liens; purchaser applies for a tax deed after redemption expires.

NE.returns: 14% per annum statutory, bid-down at some county auctions
NE.notes: County treasurer certificate sales, typically in March.

NV.redemption: None once county trustee's deed issues (2-year delinquency threshold before that)
NV.notes: County treasurer holds the property in trust, then auctions after the redemption window closes.

NH.redemption: None post-deed; New Hampshire moved to a deed/lien-hybrid tax lien statute in some municipalities post-Tyler v. Hennepin reforms
NH.returns: N/A — outright deed transfer in most municipalities
NH.notes: Municipality (not county) manages the process; procedures vary by town since 2022 legislative changes.

NJ.redemption: 2 years from sale (statutory minimum before foreclosure)
NJ.returns: Up to 18% per annum, bid down at auction; additional 2–6% penalty on larger liens
NJ.notes: Municipal-level (not county) lien sales; investor forecloses via the Superior Court to obtain title.

NM.redemption: None once the state Property Tax Division auctions the property (3-year delinquency threshold)
NM.notes: State-run (not county) auction through the Property Tax Division.

NY.redemption: Typically 2 years, varies widely by county/municipality charter
NY.returns: Varies — many counties use in-rem deed foreclosure rather than lien certificates; some (e.g., select NYC-area jurisdictions) sell liens
NY.statute: New York Real Property Tax Law Art. 11
NY.notes: Highly county/municipality-specific; check the local charter before assuming a lien or deed process applies.

NC.redemption: 10 days upset-bid period after each high bid, not a traditional redemption
NC.returns: N/A — outright deed transfer, subject to upset bids
NC.statute: North Carolina General Statutes Ch. 105, Art. 26
NC.notes: Judicial (mortgage-style) foreclosure with an upset-bid process that can extend the sale for months.

ND.redemption: 3 years from first delinquency before county takes title; county then auctions the deed
ND.returns: N/A once auctioned (county takes title first, no certificate sold to public)
ND.notes: County takes tax deed itself after the redemption period, then sells at auction — no investor-held lien certificate stage.

OH.redemption: 1 year from lien certificate sale (varies); forfeiture-to-deed track has no redemption once complete
OH.returns: Lien: up to 18% per annum, county-set
OH.notes: Larger counties run certificate (lien) sales, often via a private servicer; smaller counties more commonly go straight to a forfeited-land (deed) sale.

OK.redemption: None once the 2-year resale (deed) process completes; the initial certificate has no per-investor lien sale in most counties
OK.returns: 8% per annum accrues on the underlying tax certificate held by the county
OK.notes: County holds a certificate itself for 2 years, then holds a public resale (deed) auction — unlike states where investors buy the certificate directly.

OR.redemption: None once the county forecloses (3-year delinquency threshold before that)
OR.notes: County holds title via judgment, then auctions; some counties allow direct sale of tax-foreclosed land.

PA.redemption: None in most counties for upset/judicial sales; limited redemption (90 days) survives in specific home-rule counties (e.g., Philadelphia, in narrow cases)
PA.returns: N/A — outright deed transfer in the large majority of counties
PA.statute: Pennsylvania Real Estate Tax Sale Law, 72 P.S. §5860.101 et seq.
PA.notes: Two-tier process in many counties: upset sale (subject to liens) then judicial sale (liens stripped) for unsold parcels.

RI.returns: 10% penalty in year one, plus 1% per month after, plus costs
RI.notes: Municipal (not county) tax sale; Rhode Island has no active county government.

SC.returns: 3–12% per annum depending on when redeemed, tiered quarterly
SC.notes: County-run; often described as a 'redeemable deed' since a deed is issued at sale but subject to the redemption right and interest.

SD.redemption: 3 years from sale (varies for some parcel types)
SD.statute: South Dakota Codified Laws Ch. 10-23 to 10-25
SD.notes: County treasurer certificate sales; purchaser applies for a treasurer's deed after redemption expires.

TN.redemption: 1 year from the court's confirmation of sale (courts have discretion to extend)
TN.returns: 10% per annum statutory penalty on redemption
TN.notes: Judicial (Chancery Court) sale process run at the county level.

TX.redemption: 2 years for homestead/ag/mineral properties; 6 months for all other property
TX.returns: 25% penalty in year one, 50% in year two (homestead/ag); 25% flat for the 6-month category
TX.statute: Texas Tax Code Title 1, Subtitle E, Ch. 34
TX.notes: County (via constable/sheriff) sale; high statutory redemption penalties make this one of the most closely watched markets.

UT.redemption: None once the county auctions (4-year delinquency threshold before that)
UT.notes: County-run May auctions after the statutory delinquency period runs.

VT.redemption: 1 year from sale (town may set differently by charter)
VT.notes: Municipality-level (town), not county, since Vermont counties have no independent government function here.

VA.redemption: Right to redeem up until the court confirms the sale, not after
VA.returns: N/A — outright deed transfer once confirmed
VA.notes: Judicial in-rem sale process; independent cities function as county-equivalents in Virginia.

WA.redemption: None once the county treasurer's deed issues (3-year delinquency threshold before that)
WA.notes: County treasurer runs the foreclosure and auction directly.

WV.notes: State Auditor's office (not the county) administers delinquent-land sales for most counties.

WI.redemption: None once the county forecloses (roughly 2 years of delinquency before that)
WI.notes: County in-rem foreclosure process; some municipalities also handle their own special assessments separately.

WY.notes: County treasurer certificate sales, typically in the second week of August.

counties.redemption: 18 months from lien filing, before deed recorded
counties.returns: N/A — outright deed transfer after redemption period
counties.notes: Maine municipal tax-lien foreclosure system (not a county-run tax deed auction). In York County, each city/town files tax lien certificates in the registry; if unpaid for 18 months after filing, the lien automatically forecloses and the municipality owns the property (36 M.R.S. §943). Sale of tax-acquired property is governed by 36 M.R.S. §943-C (post-Tyler reforms): towns generally must use listed/broker processes and return surplus proceeds to the former owner. Inventory and method (listing, sealed bid, auction) vary by municipality (Sanford, Biddeford, York, Kennebunk, etc.). Unorganized territory sales shifted to licensed brokers via Maine Revenue Services.

counties.notes: Missouri redeemable-deed / certificate-of-purchase county under RSMo Chapter 140. Boone County Collector holds annual tax certificate sale fourth Monday in August at 10:00 a.m. (Roger B. Wilson Government Center Commission Chambers). Bidding starts at taxes, penalties, and costs; highest bidder wins a Certificate of Purchase — not immediate ownership. First/second offerings: generally 1-year redemption then collector's deed path with title search + 90-day certified notices; must perfect deed within 18 months of certificate or lien is lost. 10% interest on bid amount (less surplus) to purchaser on redemption; 8% on subsequent taxes paid. Non-residents need pre-arrangements with collector. 2026 sale listed August 24, 2026 with published parcel list and ArcGIS viewer.

counties.redemption: 3 years from sale (36 months)
counties.returns: 10% per annum plus penalties
counties.notes: Montana tax-lien assignment county (no competitive premium auction). Yellowstone County Treasurer attaches tax liens on the first working day of August; investors purchase assignments by mailing owners a Notice of Pending Assignment (certified mail, postmarked Aug 15 for the lottery cycle), then submitting mailing proofs, a preference-ordered Excel list, and $50 per-assignment fee by noon Aug 28. Assignments are awarded Aug 29 via county lottery (snake-method randomizer), not high bid. After Aug 29 remaining liens are first-come/first-served with 14–60 day notice. Subsequent taxes may be paid onto existing assignments June 1–July 30. Final-year process: owner-occupied residential dwellings go to public auction; other parcels issue tax deed to lienholder after statutory notice (MCA Title 15 Ch. 17–18). County recommends quiet title after tax deed.

Lottery attendance optional if payment pre-delivered by Aug 28 noon. Auction-property winners who are not the lienholder post 5% of bid or $200 (whichever greater) at sale; full payment by cash/cashier’s check within 24 hours. Tax deed fee $25 + Clerk & Recorder recording fees when deed issues.

17031.notes: Cook County runs its own annual tax sale calendar, distinct from the downstate autumn window. Sold results publish to the county open-data catalog.

26163.notes: Runs later than the state pattern, with a large second-round sale.

04013.notes: Large online February lien sale; list posts well ahead of the sale.

TX.notes: Sales are held on the first Tuesday of each month at the county courthouse. Notice must be posted at least 21 days ahead.

GA.notes: Sheriff's sales are held on the first Tuesday of the month on the courthouse steps. Advertised for four weeks beforehand. Mostly in person, so listings are often PDFs or legal-organ notices rather than a feed.

AZ.notes: Annual tax lien sale in February. Liens are bid down on the interest rate from 16%.

MI.notes: Foreclosure auctions run late summer through autumn, with a second-round sale for unsold parcels. Redemption is extinguished at the foreclosure judgment, so no post-sale redemption occurs.

FL.notes: Tax deed sales are scheduled by each clerk as applications ripen, so cadence varies by county. Most of the state runs through RealAuction, which is policy-blocked — prefer the clerk of court as source of record.

IL.notes: Annual tax sale, month varies by county (Cook runs its own calendar). Liens are bid down on the penalty rate, so the sale price is the delinquent tax owed rather than a market clearing price.

MD.notes: Annual tax sale in late spring, date set per county. High-bid-premium structure — the recorded bid is not directly comparable to a clearing price.

CA.notes: Tax-defaulted land sales are scheduled by each county, commonly spring or autumn. Sale is final; there is no post-sale right of redemption.

CO.notes: Annual lien sale in the autumn, bid up as a premium over the lien.

NJ.notes: Municipal lien sales, bid down on interest then up as premium.

IN.notes: County commissioners' certificate sales in early autumn.

TN.notes: Judicial sales scheduled by chancery court; timing varies widely.

NY.notes: In-rem foreclosure auctions run per municipality, frequently via third-party auctioneers.

OH.notes: Sheriff's sales run on a rolling docket; some counties also hold bulk lien certificate sales.

PA.notes: Upset sale in September, judicial sale later for unsold parcels.

WI.notes: County-run surplus land sales after tax deed is taken.

OR.notes: County surplus property auctions following foreclosure.

NC.notes: Judicial foreclosure sales with a 10-day upset-bid period, so the winning bid is not final at the hammer.
